result.summary: Ovid describes the Golden Age, the first of the four ages of the world. Men lived in innocence without laws, soldiers, ships or farming, and the Earth gave food freely in an eternal spring.

scenes.title: The Golden Age
scenes.summary: The narrator describes a first age of justice without laws, war or travel, where the Earth provides all food freely amid eternal spring.

notable_quotes.reason: Opens Ovid's famous picture of the Golden Age, ruled by faith and rectitude without law.
Vivid image of paradise: rivers of milk and nectar and honey from the oak.

analysis.text: The Golden Age defines a lost ideal by listing what is absent: law, punishment, war, trade and toil. It begins the decline through successive ages that runs through the early Metamorphoses.

Ovid draws on Hesiod's Works and Days and Roman ideas of a lost primitive virtue. His description of an age before ships and weapons also quietly contrasts with Augustan Rome's own claims to a new golden age.

legacy.text: Ovid's Golden Age shaped the pastoral and utopian traditions of European literature, including Renaissance poetry about Arcadia and the idea of a lost paradise.

fun_facts.text: The translation's footnotes are marked by numbers such as [28] and [29], reflecting the 19th-century prose edition with explanatory notes.

language_notes.text: Early laws were inscribed on bronze tablets and publicly displayed; the poet imagines an age that needed no such written threats.
"The pine-tree... had descended to the flowing waves" means no ships had been built; pine was the usual timber for hulls.
"Straightened" and "crooked" brass distinguish the straight trumpet (tuba) from the curved horn (cornu or lituus) used in Roman armies.
Arbute-tree is the strawberry tree; cornels are cornelian cherries. Both are wild fruits, stressing food gathered rather than farmed.
The "tree of Jove" is the oak, which was sacred to Jove (the Greek Zeus).
Zephyrs are the gentle west winds, associated with spring and growth.

context_notes.text: Ovid follows Hesiod in describing four ages of decline: Golden, Silver, Bronze and Iron. This is the first, the best.
Rivers of milk and nectar (the drink of the gods) belong to ancient visions of paradise, showing nature's effortless abundance.

literary_notes.text: The repeated negatives (no punishment, no fear, no decrees, no dread) define the age by what it lacks, stressing its purity.
The Earth is "in freedom" and "wounded" by ploughshares, treated as a living being that gives willingly rather than under compulsion.
Rivers of milk and nectar and honey dripping from trees exaggerate natural abundance to create an idealized, almost fantastical paradise.
